Family Health

Pelvic floor dysfunction: finding the right kind of treatment

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

The pelvic floor is a group of muscles and supporting tissues at the base of the pelvis. It supports pelvic organs and helps with bladder, bowel and sexual function. Problems do not always mean that the muscles need more strengthening: some muscles struggle to relax, and some do not coordinate well when needed.

What the symptoms may feel like

Possible symptoms include leaking urine or stool, difficulty emptying the bladder or bowel, pelvic pressure and pain around the pelvis, genitals or rectum. Sex may be uncomfortable or painful.

Constipation can involve straining or a sense that stool remains even after a bowel movement. A coordination problem can make it difficult for the pelvic floor to relax while the bowel tries to empty.

These symptoms are not unique to pelvic floor dysfunction. Infection, structural problems, bowel conditions and other causes may need to be considered.

Symptoms can occur in people of different sexes and at different stages of life. They are not restricted to women after childbirth, and they should not be dismissed as an unavoidable part of parenting or aging.

Some people also describe lower-back discomfort, painful urination or muscle spasms. These symptoms warrant attention to other possible causes as well; untreated symptoms do not automatically predict permanent colon damage or infection.

Weakness and excessive tension are different

A well-functioning pelvic floor needs to tighten when appropriate and then release. Muscles that remain tense may be painful and still function poorly; feeling tight does not necessarily mean they are strong.

Pregnancy, childbirth, surgery, injury and nerve problems can contribute to pelvic symptoms. Several factors may overlap, and a single cause is not always identifiable.

For some people, training strength and endurance is useful. For others, treatment begins with reducing overactivity and learning relaxation or coordination.

Doing repeated strong squeezes without assessment can be unhelpful when pain or a nonrelaxing muscle pattern is present. Conversely, saying that Kegel exercises never help would also be incorrect.

Higher body weight can add pelvic pressure, although symptoms and treatment needs cannot be judged from weight alone.

What an assessment involves

A clinician or pelvic health physiotherapist will ask about bladder and bowel habits, pain, medication, childbirth or surgery and what activities trigger symptoms. A short symptom diary can make the pattern easier to describe.

An examination may include checking movement and the abdomen, and sometimes an internal vaginal or rectal examination. The clinician should explain why it is being suggested and obtain your consent.

You can ask for a chaperone, request a pause or discuss alternatives. An internal examination is not something you must tolerate without explanation or against your wishes.

Depending on the symptoms, testing may assess urine, bladder emptying or bowel function. Sensors or pressure measurements are tools used for particular questions, not mandatory tests for every person.

A pressure sensor, sometimes called a perineometer, may be placed in the vagina or rectum for selected measurements. Surface electrodes on the perineum (the skin between the genitals and anus) can record muscle activity without the same internal approach. These measurements answer different questions and require explanation and consent.

Treatment should match the problem

Pelvic health physiotherapy may combine relaxation, breathing, movement, coordination and appropriately selected strengthening. The plan should be adjusted if an exercise increases pain or makes emptying more difficult.

Biofeedback can make muscle activity easier to understand. In certain bowel-emptying disorders, it helps retrain the coordination needed to pass stool rather than simply increasing squeezing strength.

Constipation treatment may also involve diet, fluid intake and a suitable medicine. A laxative can help stool consistency, but it does not by itself teach a muscle to relax at the right time.

Medicines for associated pain or other conditions may sometimes be useful. Muscle relaxants are not a universal first treatment and should not be started without considering their likely benefit and adverse effects.

Surgery is reserved for particular structural or other problems, such as selected prolapse conditions. It is not the usual answer to a muscle coordination problem alone.

Everyday steps that can support care

Avoid prolonged forceful straining on the toilet. Give yourself time, respond to the urge to pass stool and discuss a comfortable toileting position with your clinician or physiotherapist.

Gentle breathing and learning to release unnecessary muscle tension may help as part of an agreed plan. A warm bath can be comforting for some people, but comfort measures do not establish the cause or replace treatment.

Do not repeatedly stop the urine stream as an exercise routine. Pelvic floor training is usually practiced separately from emptying the bladder.

Keep activity within your comfort and treatment guidance. You do not need to stop all movement, but pushing through escalating pelvic pain is not a useful measure of progress.

Gentle stretches or adapted yoga may be included when comfortable and suitable. Warmth can ease discomfort, but claims about circulation do not establish that baths treat the underlying dysfunction.

Know when symptoms need urgent assessment

Seek emergency assessment for new numbness around the genitals or buttocks, new leg weakness, or sudden bladder or bowel control changes associated with back pain. These can indicate a nerve emergency rather than an ordinary exercise problem.

An inability to pass urine, severe worsening pain, fever or significant bleeding also needs prompt medical advice. Do not assume these symptoms are caused by known pelvic floor tension.

Persistent symptoms deserve a routine clinical review even when there is no emergency. Improvement can take time, but a plan should include a way to assess progress and reconsider the diagnosis if treatment is not helping.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pelvic floor dysfunction includes weakness, overactivity and coordination problems, which need different approaches.

Biofeedback and pelvic physiotherapy can help selected conditions; surgery and muscle relaxants are not universal solutions.

How BeMama can help

Use a symptom diary and request a tailored plan that explains which muscles and functions are being treated.

When to seek help

New saddle numbness, leg weakness or sudden bladder/bowel changes with back pain is an emergency; inability to urinate or severe illness also needs urgent care.

Sources and further reading

  • NIDDK — Treatment for Constipation
  • University Hospitals Plymouth NHS Trust — Pelvic Floor Relaxation

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Pelvic floor dysfunction can involve weakness, overactivity or coordination problems.
  • Exercises should be selected for the assessed problem.
  • New neurological or severe bladder symptoms need urgent care.

Frequently asked questions

Should everyone with pelvic floor symptoms do more Kegels?

No. Strengthening can help selected problems, but tense or nonrelaxing muscles may first need a different approach with pelvic health physiotherapy.

Will I need surgery?

Many people begin with conservative treatment. Surgery is considered for specific diagnosed problems, not automatically for pelvic pain or difficulty relaxing muscles.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
